Co-located Community Hubs Executive Dashboard

FY25 (1 Apr 2025 – 31 Mar 2026) · four co-located community hubs

Welcome

This dashboard tracks programming activity, reach, and space use across four Singapore community hubs — Heartbeat@Bedok, Our Tampines Hub, One Punggol, and Wisma Geylang Serai. Here's a quick guide to get you oriented.

All Hubs, then each hub

The first tab, All Hubs, carries all seven dimensions on one page — Footfall & Reach Over Time, Reach & Participation, CMIO Reach Composition, Activation & Programming Consistency, Programming Content Diversity, Festival Coverage, and Partnerships & Space — with every chart comparing the four hubs side by side. Use the list on the left to jump between dimensions. The four tabs after it are one page per hub.

Read any chart

Hover over a chart to see exact values. Most cards include a short description underneath explaining exactly what's being measured and how it's calculated — some also pose a guiding question to help frame what to look for. Each tab also opens with a Portfolio reading panel: one paragraph summarising that section's patterns, so you can get the takeaway before working through the charts.

The hub pages

Each hub has its own tab giving its full picture: background, portfolio reading, headline KPI cards, its own breakdown charts, and the complete variable table.

Meet the four hubs

Heartbeat@Bedok
Singapore's second integrated community hub, opened February 2018 (swimming complex opened a year earlier, August 2017), sited in Bedok as part of the “Remaking Our Heartland” initiative that began in 2007. It replaced the older Kampong Chai Chee Community Centre. Sits on roughly three football fields' worth of land and brings together the ActiveSG East Bedok Sports Centre (four pools, gym, tennis/badminton courts), Bedok Public Library, Kampong Chai Chee Community Club, Bedok Polyclinic, a senior care centre, and 30+ retail/F&B tenants.
One Punggol
The newest of the four (Community Club opened October 2022, full hub officially opened September 2024), reflecting Punggol's identity as one of Singapore's newest, most master-planned towns. A five-storey, 2.8-hectare building with a 600-seat multi-purpose hall, Singapore's first fully inclusive regional library (built for patrons with different abilities), a 700-seat hawker centre, childcare facilities, a kidney dialysis centre, blood collection centre, senior care, and sports facilities.
Our Tampines Hub
Singapore's first integrated lifestyle hub, and the biggest of the four (5.3 hectares). First proposed in 2011 as part of the Tampines Masterplan, shaped by consultation with 15,000+ residents, built on the old Tampines Stadium site, and opened August 2017. Houses a regional library, hawker centre, Public Service Centre, a Festive Arts Theatre, and extensive sports facilities.
Wisma Geylang Serai
Built on the site of the former Malay Village (closed 2011), explicitly conceived as the “civic, social and cultural heart” of the Geylang Serai precinct, with design blending traditional Malay house and Singapore shophouse motifs. Houses a community club, the South East CDC offices, National Arts Council arts spaces, and the Geylang Serai Heritage Gallery.

A

Footfall & Reach Over Time

How often and how consistently each hub programmes activity across the year, and how much of the calendar repeats.
Portfolio reading
All four hubs cleared their programming footfall target, but by very different margins — from 101% of target at Our Tampines Hub to 259% at Wisma Geylang Serai. Converting building visitors into programme participants is where the portfolio separates: 7.2% at Heartbeat@Bedok against 92.5% at Wisma Geylang Serai. Normalising by floor space reorders the table again — Our Tampines Hub draws the most footfall per sqm, while Wisma Geylang Serai converts space into participation most intensively at 56.5 participants per sqm, roughly 11 times the rate at One Punggol.

A hub high and to the left is getting a lot of footfall from relatively little space; a large bubble low on the chart suggests heavy foot traffic isn't yet converting into programme participation.

B

Reach & Participation

How many people programming reaches, and whether that reach comes from a few standout events or steady turnout across the board.
Portfolio reading
Reach spans a factor of 3.6 across the portfolio: Our Tampines Hub 1,006,513, Heartbeat@Bedok 460,571, Wisma Geylang Serai 292,280 and One Punggol 280,460 participants recorded in FY25. Scale and pace pull in different directions — Our Tampines Hub and Heartbeat@Bedok sit top of the table on total reach, yet the typical event ranges from just 600 people at Wisma Geylang Serai to 11,250 at Our Tampines Hub. That gap is concentration: at Wisma Geylang Serai the mean event runs 3.9 times its median, so the headline total rests on a handful of very large events, and its single biggest event alone accounts for 20% of everything the hub recorded. Our Tampines Hub is the most consistent event to event (variability 1.56); Wisma Geylang Serai the most volatile (2.07).

C

CMIO Reach Composition

Who programming reaches, broken down by ethnic group (Chinese / Malay / Indian / Other), and how evenly that reach is spread.
Portfolio reading
Chinese participants are the largest group at Heartbeat@Bedok, One Punggol and Our Tampines Hub, ranging from 56% to 69% of recorded participation. The exception is Wisma Geylang Serai, where Malay participants lead at 57%. On evenness of reach across the four groups the portfolio is tightly bunched — 0.66 at One Punggol to 0.75 at Our Tampines Hub — so no hub reaches all four groups anywhere near equally. Read these shares against each hub's catchment rather than against the national mix: a hub sited in a precinct with a distinctive population will differ by design, not by shortfall.

D

Activation & Programming Consistency

What kind of programming each hub runs by theme and by who organises it, and how varied vs. concentrated that mix is.
Portfolio reading
Programming pace splits the portfolio unevenly: Heartbeat@Bedok leads at 10.9 events a month, with Wisma Geylang Serai (10.4) and One Punggol (8.7) close behind, while Our Tampines Hub runs 2.3 — roughly 5 times fewer. Programming stopped altogether for at least one month at Our Tampines Hub (10 of 12 months active) and Wisma Geylang Serai (11 of 12 months active); the others were active in every month. One Punggol is the steadiest month to month (consistency CV 0.17, where lower is steadier) and Our Tampines Hub the most uneven (0.67). One Punggol tilts toward weekends, while Our Tampines Hub and Wisma Geylang Serai programme mainly on weekdays. Format differs just as much — single-day events run from 18% of the calendar at Our Tampines Hub to 59% at Heartbeat@Bedok, and the median event stretches to about 30 days at Our Tampines Hub. Wisma Geylang Serai leans hardest on repeat programming, with 71% of its events inside a recurring series against 21% at Our Tampines Hub.

E

Programming Content Diversity

Which of Singapore's five major festivals each hub programmes for.
Portfolio reading
Catalogue size tracks pace: Heartbeat@Bedok lists 75 distinct programmes against 28 at Our Tampines Hub. On who actually organises the programming the portfolio divides into two camps — Heartbeat@Bedok and One Punggol run largely on external partners (52%, 55% of events), while Our Tampines Hub and Wisma Geylang Serai deliver most programming in-house (79%, 75%). That shows up in organiser diversity, which runs from 0.51 at Our Tampines Hub to 0.86 at Heartbeat@Bedok; programme-type diversity is widest at Our Tampines Hub (1.00) and narrowest at Heartbeat@Bedok (0.36). By theme, each hub's largest slice is Learning & Education at Heartbeat@Bedok (24%), Celebration & Festival at One Punggol (25%), Arts & Culture at Our Tampines Hub (54%) and Arts & Culture at Wisma Geylang Serai (27%).

Festival Coverage

How footfall and participation compare to target, how they've moved over time, and how efficiently each hub converts its floor space into visitors.
Portfolio reading
Heartbeat@Bedok, One Punggol and Our Tampines Hub cover 4 of the 5 major festivals; Wisma Geylang Serai covers 2. Hari Raya and National Day are programmed at every hub. Deepavali appears at Our Tampines Hub only. Chinese New Year is missing only at Wisma Geylang Serai. Coverage is detected by keyword match on event names and description.

G

Partnerships & Space

How collaborative each hub's programming is (partnership tiers), and how its floor space is shared across co-located agencies.
Portfolio reading
Partnership depth runs from 1.62 at Wisma Geylang Serai to 2.96 at Heartbeat@Bedok on the 1–4 scale. At the deep end, Heartbeat@Bedok takes 46% of its events all the way to partner-led (Convert); at the shallow end, Wisma Geylang Serai runs 75% of its programming with no partner involved at all. Floor space differs a lot as well — 120,222 sqm at Our Tampines Hub against 14,477 sqm at Wisma Geylang Serai, an 8-fold difference How that space is shared also differs: One Punggol spreads it most evenly across its co-located agencies (0.80), while at Our Tampines Hub a single agency, SportSG, holds 51% of the floor area.

Heartbeat@BedokSingapore's second integrated community hub, opened February 2018 (swimming complex opened a year earlier, August 2017), sited in Bedok as part of the “Remaking Our Heartland” initiative that began in 2007. It replaced the older Kampong Chai Chee Community Centre. Sits on roughly three football fields' worth of land and brings together the ActiveSG East Bedok Sports Centre (four pools, gym, tennis/badminton courts), Bedok Public Library, Kampong Chai Chee Community Club, Bedok Polyclinic, a senior care centre, and 30+ retail/F&B tenants.
Portfolio reading Where this hub sits across all seven dimensions, generated from the FY25 data.
Across FY25, Heartbeat@Bedok sits highest of the four hubs on programming pace (10.9 events a month) and 2nd-highest on total participation (460,571 participants), from the 3rd-highest floor area (43,590 sqm). It leads the portfolio on programming pace, organiser diversity and partnership depth, and is joint-highest on festival coverage. It sits last of the four on programme-type diversity — the clearest place to look for headroom. A high share of its programming is partner-led rather than run in-house, so its calendar depends materially on the strength of those external relationships.

Our Tampines HubSingapore's first integrated lifestyle hub, and the biggest of the four (5.3 hectares). First proposed in 2011 as part of the Tampines Masterplan, shaped by consultation with 15,000+ residents, built on the old Tampines Stadium site, and opened August 2017. Houses a regional library, hawker centre, Public Service Centre, a Festive Arts Theatre, and extensive sports facilities.
Portfolio reading Where this hub sits across all seven dimensions, generated from the FY25 data.
Across FY25, Our Tampines Hub sits lowest of the four hubs on programming pace (2.3 events a month) and highest on total participation (1,006,513 participants), from the highest floor area (120,222 sqm). It leads the portfolio on total participation, typical event size, evenness of ethnic reach and programme-type diversity, and is joint-highest on festival coverage. It sits last of the four on programming pace, month-to-month steadiness, organiser diversity, delivery against footfall target and share of programming in recurring series — the clearest place to look for headroom. Its reach is concentrated: mean participation per event runs well above the median, so headline totals rest on a handful of very large events rather than steady week-to-week turnout.

Wisma Geylang SeraiBuilt on the site of the former Malay Village (closed 2011), explicitly conceived as the “civic, social and cultural heart” of the Geylang Serai precinct, with design blending traditional Malay house and Singapore shophouse motifs. Houses a community club, the South East CDC offices, National Arts Council arts spaces, and the Geylang Serai Heritage Gallery.
Portfolio reading Where this hub sits across all seven dimensions, generated from the FY25 data.
Across FY25, Wisma Geylang Serai sits 2nd-highest of the four hubs on programming pace (10.4 events a month) and 3rd-highest on total participation (292,280 participants), from the lowest floor area (14,477 sqm). It leads the portfolio on delivery against footfall target, participation per sqm of floor space and share of programming in recurring series. It sits last of the four on typical event size, festival coverage and partnership depth — the clearest place to look for headroom. Its reach is concentrated: mean participation per event runs well above the median, so headline totals rest on a handful of very large events rather than steady week-to-week turnout.
